text: The seduction goes in order: first the wife, then the husband, then all three of them into burglary. Bob finds the couple mid-argument in a bar, ends the fight, and proceeds through the marriage as though it were a corridor with two doors. Bertrand Blier plays this as comedy and holds it to eighty-four minutes, roughly the attention span of the arrangement itself; the jokes are structural rather than verbal, since what is funny is how little the respectable version of that marriage was worth to the people inside it. Nobody is granted dignity and nobody is punished. The burglaries that follow are less a plot than a way of keeping three people busy while they work out what they have agreed to. A César went to the actress at the center of it, which is where the damage collects.

The villa in Saint Tropez belongs to one of them; the other is a guest whose welcome can be withdrawn. That imbalance is set in the opening minutes, when a rich woman stops in front of a street artist's work, pays for it, and takes the artist south with her, and Claude Chabrol never lets it out of the frame. When an architect turns up and both women want him, the film becomes a quiet accounting of who can afford to lose, and the lead performance carrying that accounting took a Silver Bear. The manner is what unsettles: Chabrol films the household with the flat courtesy of a man documenting a well-run establishment, so the pressure arrives disguised as hospitality and the guest learns what she must become in order to stay. Nothing raises its voice.

Two men are on a ship early in the twentieth century, and one of them has a story he needs a stranger to hear. The Italian talks; the Russian listens; the 121 minutes belong almost entirely to a man arranging his own past for someone with no way to check any of it. Dark Eyes was produced in Italy in 1987 by a Russian director and plays largely in Russian, which gives that simple frame a second floor: the confession crosses a border as well as a table, and keeps having to translate itself for the person it has chosen. Nikita Mikhalkov lets the comedy sit near the surface, since the teller is good company and knows it, while the shape underneath is the plainer one of a life being edited in front of a witness. The listener's silence does much of the work.

A young Austrian is delivered to Versailles as a term of agreement between two countries that dislike each other. Everything in the 149 minutes that follow proceeds from that transaction: a marriage to a future king who chose it no more than she did, a court whose rules she is expected to have known on arrival, and a habit of spending that begins as compensation and hardens into character. The film was built in 1938 at the scale the subject invited, and its score and production design drew Academy attention, a fair index of where the budget went. The friction is that the picture enjoys the extravagance it will later hold against her; the silks are photographed with appetite and then handed to a hostile public as evidence. W.S. Van Dyke keeps the politics at the level of household management, which is where a queen of that court would have met them.

Three women share a maternity ward, and none of them chose the company. Ingmar Bergman keeps nearly the whole of these eighty-five minutes inside that room, where the day runs on a schedule none of the patients set and the only privacy on offer is what the others agree not to notice. The chamber form does something specific here: three separate crises, each of which would carry a film on its own, are made to share the same walls, so one woman's hope reaches the next bed sounding like a threat. The recognition the film received was for its acting, which is the honest place for it, since the camera has nowhere to go but faces. Nothing is arranged as a symbol. There is a body, a bed, and the hours the ward keeps.

A woman who has not driven in years takes the car out because there is nobody else to do it. Chela's partner has gone to prison on fraud charges, and the arrangements of a shared life have to be rebuilt around one person; the elderly women of her circle need lifts and will pay for them, so an unplanned taxi route becomes the first work she has done alone as an adult. Marcelo Martinessi keeps everything at domestic scale — a bell that has to be answered, a passenger collected at an agreed hour, a house that suddenly has to pay for itself — and the lead performance took a Silver Bear. Then Angy gets into the car, much younger and unimpressed by any of it, and the film's attention moves from what has been taken away to what Chela still wants at an age when wanting is presumed finished.

A deserter cannot be hired, and that fact does more damage here than any amount of disapproval. Elvira Madigan is an acrobat whose name audiences know; Sixten Sparre is an officer with a wife, two children, and a commission he walks away from. Bo Widerberg treats the elopement as the easy part and gives his ninety-one minutes to what comes after, which is two people outside every arrangement that used to feed them, learning how quickly a summer has to be paid for. The romance is not undercut so much as costed. Widerberg lets their pleasure in each other stay genuine — this is not a film that punishes anyone for happiness — while the practical ground underneath thins out week by week, and neither of them has anywhere to put that information.

Seven children, and Jo is leaving a second husband in order to marry a third. Jake writes screenplays, does well at it, and is unfaithful as a matter of routine; the two of them are matched in precisely the ways that do not survive a decade of practice. Jack Clayton made the film in Britain in 1964, and what holds is how little of Jo's own life is hers to narrate — the children arrive, the work supplies the calendar, and her wanting anything is treated by everyone near her as a condition to be managed rather than a position to be argued with. It proceeds by accumulation rather than crisis: a conversation that does not conclude, a decision taken on her behalf, a household that runs. The Academy recognition the film drew went to its lead performance, the only place it could have gone.

His affairs are a habit everyone has agreed to tolerate; hers would be an incident. Paula Tessier runs her own business in Paris and has spent years with a man who keeps starting over with younger women, so when the twenty-five-year-old son of a client makes his interest plain she refuses him, and then, at the least convenient moment, does not. Anatole Litvak shot this in France in 1961, in English, and the sharp part is not the affair but the bookkeeping around it: what a room will forgive turns out to vary precisely with who is doing the thing. No verdict is delivered aloud. The pressure arrives as tone, in a slight adjustment to how she is addressed and a shift in what is considered amusing, and the film is unhurried enough to let her feel it gathering before she can name it.

Mangin collects information the way a bad landlord collects rent. Maurice Pialat's inspector leans on informants, bloodies suspects, and then takes up with a woman he arrested, and Police spends most of its 113 minutes in rooms where nothing cinematic is happening: a desk, a corridor, a bar, the same question asked again with less patience. The drug case against three brothers is genuine, and Pialat keeps losing interest in it on purpose. What holds him is a man whose whole professional method is coercion finding that he wants something he cannot requisition, from a woman with a far better sense of leverage than he has. A Volpi Cup for the lead is the tidiest thing about the picture; everything else has the unfinished quality of work that will still be there tomorrow.

A car with two women in it who have just met, pointed at a border. Rebecca has been in Jerusalem a few months and has just ended her engagement; Hanna is driving, and Hanna is not going anywhere near where Rebecca meant to go, because she is crossing into Jordan, to the Free Zone, to collect a large sum of money. Amos Gitai keeps the ninety minutes largely in the front seats, so the region arrives as windshield, checkpoint and delay rather than as position, and the two of them have to conduct their business at the speed of traffic. The errand is the substance: money owed, someone to collect it from, a line on a map that separates the parties officially and not much otherwise. Neither woman's trouble makes room for the other's, and the drive does not resolve that so much as continue.

What the court cannot forgive is not only whom the king loves but what he keeps handing him. Edward gives Piers Gaveston, a man of no birth at all, the titles the great families understood to be theirs by arrangement, and out of that grievance a queen and the man she conspires with assemble a case that never needs to mention affection. Derek Jarman compresses the fourteenth century into ninety minutes and treats the distance as thin: the complaint is administrative, the language is blunt, and men do sums in land and office while calling the result honor. Isabella is the coldest thing in the film and the most interesting, and the Volpi Cup went to the actress playing her, for a part that has to hold a genuinely displaced wife and a strategist in the same body. Gaveston's standing, meanwhile, is worth exactly what the king's attention is worth.

Cleuza cleans an apartment on the far side of São Paulo from the house where her sons sleep, and the distance between those two addresses is most of the film. She is pregnant again. Each of her sons has a father nobody names, and the eldest, Dênis, spends his days delivering across the same city by motorcycle while a small son of his own lives somewhere else. Daniela Thomas gives each of them a separate errand and lets the errands run at once, so the household is assembled only at the edges of a day, in the hour before work and the hour after it. Nothing is set up as a lesson about the periphery. What accumulates instead is a plain sense of how much motion is required to hold one family in place, and how little of that motion anyone in it gets to choose.

The things Isadora Duncan scandalized her public with included free love, Soviet sympathies, and unpaid bills. Karel Reisz takes 131 minutes over a dancer who changed what ballet was permitted to look like, and he declines to sort her offenses into the serious and the trivial: the debts sit beside the politics, the dress beside the lovers, all of it one continuous argument about what a body may do in public. The National Board of Review placed the film among the year's ten best. What keeps it from settling into the usual arc is that Reisz gives the dancing and the money equal weight and explains neither, so a woman working barefoot and half-dressed makes a claim her creditors and her admirers receive as the same claim. The form generally promises an account of how someone became themselves. This one keeps her company instead.
